lines.text: A leaf page can only hold a handful of entries before it fills up.
Insert one more into a page that's already full. What actually happens to it?
It splits, genuinely.
Its entries divide into two pages, and a new key gets handed up to the parent.
Run it for real: inserting past a full page genuinely allocated a brand-new page and pushed a real separator key up into a new root.
Every one of the original keys is still found correctly, right where it should be, after the split.
Keep inserting records, thousands more of them.
Does the structure need to grow a new level for roughly every batch of records, or does something else keep it from growing that fast?
Much slower, genuinely.
A high enough fanout per page keeps the whole structure only a few levels deep.
Run it for real: after thousands of inserts, the structure's own depth genuinely stayed within a handful of levels.
Every one of those thousands of records is still found correctly by walking down from the root.
Take two trees and feed them the identical sequence of inserts.
One of them deliberately leaves each page less than completely full before its next split; the other packs pages fuller.
Which one ends up splitting more times, over that same identical sequence?
The one packed less full, genuinely.
Each of its splits leaves less spare room, so the very next insert forces another split sooner.
Run it for real: packing pages less full genuinely caused more splits over the identical insert sequence than packing them fuller did.
The same inserts, two different outcomes, purely from how much slack each split leaves behind.
A split's new separator key only has one job: tell the left side apart from the right side.
Can that separator genuinely take less storage than a full copy of the key, and still send every search to the correct side?
Yes, genuinely.
Keeping only the part where the two sides first actually differ is enough to route correctly.
Run it for real: a separator built from only the first differing part of the key genuinely took fewer bytes than a full copy of that key.
Yet it routed every single test key exactly the way the full key would have.
One real production system documents exactly this technique, in its own source tree, in plain terms.

It states the entire point of throwing away those extra, unneeded key bytes directly: doing that is what lets each page hold more separators, so the whole structure branches wider and stays shallower.
So here's the shape of this whole topic: a page that fills up doesn't refuse a new entry, it splits, and that split is what makes room for the structure to keep growing correctly.
A high branching factor per page is exactly what keeps that growth from ever costing many levels, even once the record count reaches into the billions.

And two smaller decisions compound on top of that: leaving a little slack in each page on purpose means fewer splits later, and trimming a separator key down to only its first real difference means every one of those splits costs less to remember.
